what_its_for: Albumin Human is a protein solution given through an IV (intravenous) line in a hospital or clinic setting. It is used to restore and maintain blood volume when you have lost a large amount of fluid due to serious burns, surgery, trauma, liver disease (such as cirrhosis), kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome), or other serious medical conditions. It helps keep fluid in your blood vessels where it belongs and supports your blood pressure.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a nurse or doctor through an IV line directly into your vein. You will NOT give this medication to yourself at home. The infusion is given slowly over a period of time determined by your doctor. You will be monitored carefully during the infusion for any reactions. Do NOT try to inject or take this medication on your own.
dosing: Your dose is completely determined by your doctor based on your medical condition, body weight, blood pressure, and how well your body is responding to treatment. Doses vary widely from person to person. You may receive one dose or several doses over multiple days while you are in the hospital. Your medical team will decide the exact amount and how fast it is given.
missed_dose: Because this medication is given in a hospital or clinical setting by healthcare professionals, you will not manage your own doses at home. If you have concerns about your treatment schedule or feel a dose was missed or delayed, speak directly with your doctor or nurse right away.
storage: You do not need to store this medication at home. In the clinical setting, Albumin Human is stored at room temperature between 68°F and 86°F (20°C to 30°C). It should not be frozen. The solution must be clear and slightly yellowish in color — it should never be used if it looks cloudy, has particles floating in it, or if the bottle seal has been broken. Once opened, the solution must be used right away and any leftover amount must be safely discarded.
what_to_avoid: Tell your healthcare team about ALL medications, supplements, and herbal products you take, as some may interact with albumin. Avoid getting up too quickly after the infusion, as you may feel dizzy. Do not eat or drink anything that your doctor has told you to restrict, especially if you are on a fluid or sodium-restricted diet, since some albumin products contain sodium. Avoid alcohol and inform your team if you smoke, as these can affect your condition.
when_to_call_doctor: Tell your nurse or doctor IMMEDIATELY during or after your infusion if you experience: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness or chest pain, rapid or irregular heartbeat, sudden drop or rise in blood pressure, fever, chills, or shaking, skin rash, hives, itching, or flushing, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, nausea or vomiting, dizziness or fainting, unusual back or chest pain, or feeling like your heart is racing or pounding. These could be signs of a serious allergic reaction or fluid overload and need immediate attention.
when_it_works: Albumin Human begins working relatively quickly — often within minutes to hours of starting the infusion. Your blood pressure and fluid levels may begin to stabilize during or shortly after the infusion. Your medical team will monitor your vital signs, lab values, and overall response throughout your treatment to know if it is working as expected.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and above): May be more sensitive to fluid changes and should be monitored extra carefully for signs of fluid overload, such as swelling or difficulty breathing. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Should inform their doctor, as albumin is generally considered safe in pregnancy when medically necessary, but your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks. Children: Doses are carefully adjusted based on the child's weight and condition and are administered only in a medical setting. People with heart, kidney, or liver problems: Must be monitored very closely, as this medication can affect fluid and salt balance in the body. People with anemia or low clotting factors: May need additional treatments alongside albumin.
